source: Washington State University - Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center (WSU-TFREC)
title: Powdery Mildew of Stone Fruits (Podosphaera clandestina) on Sweet and Tart Cherry
content: Cherry powdery mildew, caused by the obligate biotrophic ascomycete Podosphaera clandestina (formerly Sphaerotheca pannosa var. persicae; anamorph Oidium cerasi), is one of the two pre-harvest fungal diseases limiting sweet cherry production in dry semi-arid growing regions (WA, OR, ID, Chile, Argentina, South Africa, southeastern Australia, Turkey, Spain). Unlike many powdery mildews P. clandestina causes direct fruit infection producing russeting, discoloration, and unmarketable fruit on all cultivars; susceptibility highest on Bing, Lambert, Van, Rainier, Chelan; Regina, Kordia, Skeena are moderately resistant. P. clandestina infects young rapidly expanding leaves (especially new extension shoot growth), green fruit, and pedicels. Initial foliar symptoms are faintly chlorotic angular mottled areas on lower leaf surface; after 3-5 days a delicate sparse white web-like mycelial mat with conidiophores and chains of barrel-shaped conidia develops on BOTH leaf surfaces. Infected leaves are distorted, puckered, cupped upward at edges, remain small; severely infected terminal growth is stunted and rosetted. Green fruit infection causes net-like powdery mildew russeting that destroys glossy skin required for fresh-market packout; fruit may also crack at the suture due to uneven epidermal expansion and can abort in heavy infections during shuck-fall/pit-hardening stages. P. clandestina overwinters as tiny spherical 100-140 um dark brown/black cleistothecia (chasmothecia with dichotomously branched appendages) on fallen leaves and in 1-3 year old wood bark crevices. In spring around tight cluster to white bud stage, mature chasmothecia absorb water and split open releasing a single ascus containing 8 ascospores; discharge occurs during light wetting periods at temperatures suitable for primary infection of first unfolding leaves. Once primary lesions produce conidia, secondary cycles repeat every 5-8 days at 20-25 C; P. clandestina is uniquely problematic in dry WSU production areas because free water is NOT required for conidial infection (optimum RH 50-70%). Efficient latent mycelial nursery budwood carryover also spreads propagation. Management: (1) avoid over-fertilization with nitrogen, avoid excessive pruning that promotes succulent highly-susceptible shoot growth; (2) chasmothecia sanitation: urea (40 lb N/acre) on fallen autumn leaves plus flail-mow leaf litter; remove heavily infected 2-year-old cankers during dormant pruning; (3) WSU Cherry Powdery Mildew Prediction Model calculates daily index from temperature and RH, sprays triggered when accumulated daily index reaches 100 (typically white bud/first cover in WA); (4) standard high-risk cultivar program: 2 early-season micronized/dusting sulphur (FRAC M2) sprays at white bud and full bloom; 4-5 mid-season sprays alternating FRAC 3 DMI (tebuconazole, fenbuconazole, metconazole, myclobutanil), FRAC U8 (fluopyram), FRAC 7 (metrafenone), FRAC 50 (cyflufenamid), FRAC 13 (quinoxyfen); 1 post-harvest spray on late-season shoot growth. In organic orchards, elemental sulfur (avoid within 2 weeks of oil or >30 C) alternating with potassium bicarbonate, Regalia (Reynoutria sachalinensis extract), and Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 (Serenade) biopesticides provide 50-75% control compared to the best synthetic DMI programs.
